How it looked

Everything around you, 1700 years ago

  • This is a model of ancient Rome.
  • The round building is the Colosseum.
  • All the ruins you see were once parts of this busy city.

The Colosseum

The big one

  • Opened in AD 80. About 50,000 people sat here.
  • They watched gladiator fights and wild animal hunts. Entry was free.
  • Under the floor were tunnels and lifts. Animals came up through trapdoors.

Arch of Constantine

Next to the Colosseum, toward the Palatine

  • Built in AD 315 for Emperor Constantine.
  • It celebrates his win in a civil war.
  • Many of the sculptures were taken from older monuments and reused.

Meta Sudans (low round ruin)

Small circle of stones between the Arch and the Colosseum

  • This was a big cone-shaped fountain. Water ran down its sides.
  • It stood for 1800 years.
  • In 1936 it was removed to make a road. Only the base is left.

Ludus Magnus – gladiator school

East of the Colosseum, on the street side

  • This was the biggest training school for gladiators.
  • They lived and practised here in a small arena.
  • A tunnel led straight into the Colosseum.

Domus Aurea – Nero's Golden House

Under the park on the hill north of the Colosseum (Colle Oppio)

  • After the great fire of AD 64, Emperor Nero built a huge palace here.
  • It had a big lake where the Colosseum stands now.
  • Later emperors filled it in and built over it. Today it is underground. You can visit with a tour.

Temple of Venus and Roma

The raised platform between the Colosseum and the Forum

  • The largest temple of ancient Rome. Built by Emperor Hadrian around AD 135.
  • Two goddesses, back to back: Venus (love) and Roma (the city).
  • The bushes on the platform mark where the columns stood.

Arch of Titus

At the top of the road into the Forum

  • Built around AD 81 for Emperor Titus.
  • It remembers his capture of Jerusalem in AD 70.
  • Inside, a carving shows soldiers carrying the Temple's menorah (big candle holder).

The Roman Forum

The valley full of ruins west of the Colosseum

  • The heart of the city.
  • Romans came here to shop, go to court, vote, hear speeches and pray.
  • Over the centuries it was buried and forgotten. It was dug up again in the 1800s–1900s.

Basilica of Maxentius

Three giant brick arches on the Forum's north side

  • Built AD 308–312. The biggest building in the Forum.
  • A "basilica" was not a church. It was a hall for courts and business.
  • What you see is only one side. The middle was even taller.

Temple of Antoninus and Faustina

Columns with a church behind them

  • Emperor Antoninus built it in AD 141 for his dead wife Faustina.
  • Later a church was built inside it.
  • That is why it survived so well.

Temple of Vesta

Small round temple in the Forum

  • Six priestesses, the Vestal Virgins, kept a sacred fire burning here.
  • Romans believed if the fire went out, Rome was in danger.
  • The women lived next door, in the House of the Vestals.

Temple of Castor and Pollux

Three tall columns standing alone

  • For the twin gods Castor and Pollux.
  • Romans believed the twins helped them win a battle in 495 BC.
  • The temple also checked weights and measures for traders.

Curia – Senate House

Tall plain brick building

  • The Roman Senate met here. Started by Julius Caesar.
  • It became a church in the 600s. That saved it.
  • Inside, the original marble floor is still there.

Arch of Septimius Severus

Big arch at the far end of the Forum

  • Built in AD 203.
  • It celebrates the emperor's wins in wars in the East (today's Iraq).

Temple of Saturn

Eight columns at the far end

  • One of the oldest temples in Rome (first built about 497 BC).
  • It held the state treasury – Rome's gold and silver.
  • Its winter festival, Saturnalia, had parties and gifts.

Palatine Hill

The green hill south-west of the Colosseum

  • Legend says Rome was founded here by Romulus.
  • Rich Romans, then emperors, built their homes here.
  • The word "palace" comes from "Palatine".

Circus Maximus

Long grassy field behind the Palatine

  • A huge stadium for chariot races.
  • Around 150,000 people could watch.
  • Today it is a park. Some ruins remain at the curved end.
